speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to offer a few remarks on Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof. In considering this Bill it is necessary to start from the basic and fundamental starting point of our national debt, that horrendous figure, that tragic legacy of the previous administration. It is almost impossible to overstate the magnitude and seriousness of that Liberal legacy. Not only did we inherit the debt, we also inherited a Government financial operation that is completely out of control. The problem has been created because successive Liberal administrations over the years believed in deficits of ever-growing proportions regardless of the state of the economy. Thirty to 40 per cent cost over-runs were a matter of course because of financial incompetence and indifference. Year after year this is what was served up to the Canadian people, a terrible legacy for this and future generations. We were elected to deal with this situation, Mr. Speaker, and deal with it we shall.
I will not bore you with statistics, Mr. Speaker. The House has heard often enough the price that current and future generations will have to pay for this lamentable legacy. We have heard of the amount owed by every man, woman, and child in this country for past spending excesses and how interest alone on the accumulated debt exceeds the total budget of a few short years ago.
I want to address solutions to this problem. We have to come to grips with our national debt in exactly the same way as one reduces a personal debt. We either achieve a higher income, reduce expenditures, or seek a combination of the two. This combination of the two mechanisms is what we proposed in the May Budget; increased federal income, partly through
tax changes, on the one hand, and reduced federal expenditures on the other. It is important to recognize that action to increase revenue accounts for only 20 per cent of this year's attack on the deficit. Bill C-80 is but one part of a comprehensive approach the Government has initiated to break the financial hemorrhage we inherited in September, 1984.
Opposition spokesmen have sung a song about ordinary Canadians at every opportunity. They would have you and others, Mr. Speaker, believe that they and they alone speak for ordinary Canadians. Indeed, it was the ordinary Canadians, the many responsible and caring voters in this country, who cried "enough" just over a year ago. By the hundreds of thousands they threw out the tired and incompetent Liberal Government, rejected their fellows in arms, the NDP, and elected a Progressive Conservative Government which pledged to raise revenues, control spending, reduce the deficit and create jobs. This is exactly what we are doing, Mr. Speaker. We are keeping our campaign commitment on this issue as we have in the many other important policy areas.
Spending money is easy, Mr. Speaker. Our predecessors showed all of Canada just how good they were at spending money. Never mind any controls, think of a spending program and we will give you the money. Do not worry about accountability or prudence, there is more money where this came from. Their NDP colleagues chortled with joy. We have been witnessing a spending binge for over a decade, each encouraging the other with their spending zeal.

The inflation rate is steady at just under 4 per cent, business confidence is up in the past six months, the investment rate is up, housing starts have increased and consumer spending is up. Can the opposition Parties be opposed to all these important financial indicators? Canadians are not opposed to it.
In part, this improvement in the past 12 months, which is at least welcome on this side of the House, is the result of actions taken by the Government. Another important ingredient in this welcome change is the anticipation of stated government intentions, competent financial management and deficit control.
Earlier in this debate, Members opposite lamented the amount of money these tax measures in Bill C-80 would take from ordinary Canadians. As usual, they put forward very selective arguments and did not mention some of the offsetting benefits Canadians have received as part of the Government's actions. They include lower interest rates, over 300,000 new jobs, pensions for widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64, new increased pensions for the handicapped, increased pensions for veterans, substantial new funds for direct job creation and training, and funding for record-sized ERDA agreements with the provinces. There is a whole range of initiatives of direct benefit to Canadians in all walks of life. These are actions which have injected money and confidence into the economy.
Members on the other side have complained that Bill C-80 is a tax on the poor. However, they conveniently ignore the fact that the Government has invoked a surtax on the rich and will shortly introduce a Bill for a minimum tax, to commence in January, 1986, to ensure that all Canadians will pay a fair share of tax in the future. The Liberal Party, for all its years in office, did not have the wit or inclination to deal with this important matter. As well, we have introduced a surtax on corporations and a surtax on large banks and trust companies. All of these measures were contained in the May Budget. Since the Opposition is so negative, must one conclude that it is opposed to these measures as well?
Bill C-80 is an essential stage in restoring sensible fiscal management to our nation's affairs. The opposition Parties have shown considerable ingenuity in developing spending programs and indeed I will not deny that some of their ideas over the years have been good. We have endorsed some of them. Unfortunately, the Opposition does not seem to know how to raise funds adequately, sensibly and prudently and
certainly how to account for these funds once they have been raised. Spending money is easy and oftentimes popular. Raising money tends to be unpopular and contentious. Nevertheless, it is an essential part of responsible Government, and responsible people must take responsible action to discharge this essential obligation.
Bill C-80 does that. It is a necessary response to the budgetary needs of this country. It is a proposal maligned by the unthinking and regretfully acknowledged as necessary by the rest. Bill C-80 is just one step in a long vital journey back to the economic safe ground where our massive debt can be brought under control, where competent and responsible fiscal management is restored to this country and where Canadians, after a number of years of uncertainty and doubt, can look forward to financial security for themselves and their families wherever they may live in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. There are several comments I would like to make in reply.

First, I again draw to the Hon. Member's attention the fact that Bill C-80 and the proposed tax measures are a part of the 20 per cent reduction in the deficit for this year. To suggest that Bill C-80 is the only measure that has been taken is, of course, quite wrong.
There is, indeed, a place in the scheme of things for deficit budgeting. Unhappily, the previous administration, over a great many years in good times and bad, indulged in that practice. If deficit budgeting had been properly co-ordinated and organized so that it was genuinely benefiting the Canadian economy, there might have been some purpose to it. But when you start getting 50 per cent cost overruns year after year to the point, as I emphasized earlier, that just interest payments on the debt are more than the whole budget of a few years ago, clearly corrective action has to be taken. If deficit spending was all that successful, why are we in the mess we are today? No control is the reason.
It is essential that revenues be raised to pay the debt and to pay for ongoing expenses. This Bill is an attempt to spread the load evenly. Action is being taken prudently, and in many instances phased in. It is irresponsible to do otherwise.
The Opposition has had a lot to say about proposed spending reductions, trimmings and cuts, and does not like any of them. That, however, is an essential part of the budgetary process. The additional revenues are only 20 per cent of the approach in this fiscal year to deal with the monumental problem that we have inherited.

What is also not taken into account by the Government is that there are provinces in this nation that have provincial taxes that are as high as 22 per cent. Someone living in Newfoundland is hit worse by the Budget than someone living in another province of Canada. It is estimated that Newfoundlanders have to pay again 50 per cent of the taxes imposed under this Bill. Surely that is not fair. The Bill is not fair to all Canadians.
The same thing applies to the changes in income tax. When filling out one's income tax form, one first fills out federal tax payable and then provincial tax payable as a percentage of federal tax payable. When a change is made to the federal tax payable, it influences the provincial tax payable. In provinces like Newfoundland with high provincial income tax, one ends up paying even more provincial income tax. This is how the budgetary measures brought in by the Government provide a windfall for the provincial administrations as well as the federal administration.
Canadians in the poorer provinces who have to pay double what people in other provinces have to pay because of the provincial take on the bottom line, whether in income tax or sales tax, wonder what the Government is doing. Those people see the Government spending $1 billion here and $1 billion there with only a sweep of the pen. The spending of this money occurred because of an on-the-spot decision made by the Minister of Finance or the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) under the direction of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in a private meeting held on a Saturday afternoon while the economic conference was going on and the TV cameras were rolling. According to the 1984 annual review by the Economic Council of Canada-by no means a radical body, a socialist body or a bunch of crazies-we can collect in addition between $30 billion and $50 billion a year from corporations. Mr. Speaker, our task today as Members of the Progressive Conservative Party is, of course, not a very cheerful one. Asking people to make sacrifices is never an easy thing to do. However, considering the financial situation we inherited from the previous Government, we had, need I say it again, no choice. What makes our task even more difficult is the realization, and I hope I can say this calmly, that the Members of the previous Government had created an untenable situation in this country, as a result of poor financial management, lack of interest in the economy, a complete absence of administrative skills and their chronic fear of taking action to contain inflation because they were afraid to arouse the displeasure of the people, and all this for the sole purpose of maintaining their little kingdom, and there was also their increasing tendency distributing favours, thus aiding and abetting the kind of bandaid policies they incorporated into the system for over fifteen years, with their legendary arrogance which deprived
this country of the views of all its economic and social partners.
For more than fifteen years, as a result of their absurd phobia, their incredible excuse that all the ills of this country were to be blamed on nationalists, whether they were from Quebec or anywhere else in Canada, and by their legendary but ill-famed skill in focussing the attention of the media on artificial problems while the real ones were waiting desperately for solutions, yes, Mr. Speaker, those people, and I hope no one will ever forget it, plunged this country into the morass from which it is now emerging, thanks to the responsible attitude of this Government's Members.
Mr. Speaker, we are not talking through our hats. In less than one year and a half, we have done more for Canadians than the so-called New-Liberal-Democrats managed to do in fifteen years.
During the election campaign, Mr. Speaker, we had promised to shift into reverse and get rid of those famous hand-out programs which had made a good many Canadians rely exclusively on their good old paternalistic Members of Parliament. Those popular programs had undermined the creative vitality of our country's most innovative, most promising and most sacred resource, our youths, programs which practically eliminated all retraining opportunities for workers in their forties who had just lost their jobs because the Government, totally unimaginative as it was, simply could not bring itself to get off the beaten path.
Mr. Speaker, this Government is extremely proud to have completely destroyed all such remnants of the mental atrophy of pseudo-Jesuits.
Our Government strongly believed that Canadians were determined to build a new country, a country which is not afraid to take bold steps, a country which affords every citizen the opportunity to open up a new career, which gives its people the incentive to start up new businesses and provides them with the proper tools to shed fears created by ignorance and generated by paternalism.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) rose to the challenge and did get off the beaten path. She expressed full confidence in the private sector. She knew she could count on the intelligence of youths and Canadians generally, and she simply would not baby them as the previous Government had done. Well, Mr. Speaker, she did live up to the challenge, and how!
The programs we now have cannot in any way be considered as crutches one must carry throughout life, for they are indeed stepping stones towards the kind of training which is absolutely essential in our days.
Mr. Speaker, I have not lost sight of the issue as I speak these words because, sure enough, every good thing has its price, and Canadians were aware of this when they elected us. No Government, even if I am willing to render unto Caligula

the things which are Caligula's, can deny its responsibility for a disaster simply by passing the buck. It should act and try, as a good Government, with all the resources at its disposal and the cooperation of the people in all walks of life, to find the best and cheapest solutions, especially if it assumed power at a time when the country was on the brink of bankruptcy.
Mr. Speaker, this Government having decided to act with, I repeat, the consent of the Canadian people, it has felt that a tax increase on various commodities was the price to pay to help our economy recover. I said the Government had the consent of the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker, because in the September 1984 election, the Canadian people clearly demonstrated to our hon. friends opposite that they had lost faith in their quack remedies, that they did not believe that they could reduce the deficit with quasi-usurious interest rates, with uncontrolled unemployment, with an elitist, arrogant and despising attitude, by encouraging a number of provinces at the expense of others, and with the narrow-mindedness of their elected representatives. No, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people clearly demonstrated that they had reached the age of political maturity, that they realized finally that those who borrow money must pay it back sooner or later, and that if we did not reimburse what we owe, we would jeopardize forever our future.
Because it wants very strongly to put Canada back on the right track again, the Government will not surrender its responsibilities simply to make political gains as the former Liberal administration tried to, because it was in utter disarray. The Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced in his Budget that Canada would no longer bury its head in the sand and that it would make a voluntary collective effort to get out of the hole.
It is the mark of a good leader and a good people when, together, they decide to apply difficult but effective constraints to put their country back on track. Such an attitude can only lead to success.

Mr. Speaker, what Bill C-80 tells us, as it is an integral part of this Budget, is that, if the Government really tries to balance the tax burden and to make it more equitable, each citizen will also have to be willing to do his fair share of this national economic readjustment effort. Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform Hon. Members of the decisions that were reached yesterday by the Survival Committee to prevent the shutdown of six plants in Eastern Montreal and the loss of 5,000 jobs.
First, members of the Survival Committee of Eastern Montreal are asking to meet the Prime Minister in order to explain the situation and suggest steps he should take to prevent the shutting down of those plants.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall to the attention of the House the plight of the adherents of the Baha'i faith living in Iran. The persecution of Baha'is in Iran died down in 1983, with world outrage being expressed over the hanging of 10 Baha'i women and girls simply for teaching their religion to the youth of their community.
We are now told that the imprisonment, torture, and executions of Baha'is have resumed once again on a large scale. Let us and our Government not be silent on this grave matter, for the Government of Iran may be looking to eradicate its Baha'i population.
The Baha'i religion, with its origins in Persia, is the largest religious minority in Iran with 300,000 members residing there. Their doctrine forbids involvement in politics. Canada was the first country in the world to speak out on this issue in the past, unanimously passing parliamentary resolutions through the House on July 16, 1980, and June 9, 1981, in support of the Baha'is in Iran. The Canadian delegation to the United Nations has also actively pursued the matter there, and Canada has been open to refugees from the area.
We in the New Democratic Party call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to do what they can through their offices to impress upon Iran that Canada wants to see the repression of the Baha'is in Iran stopped. We ask the Government to pay close attention to the report of the special representative on human rights to the UN General Assembly pertaining to this matter, which is expected to be released in late November or early December.

Head of the Church in Quebec for 34 years and Primate of Canada, Cardinal Roy served the Church and society with great intelligence, dedication and a mind open to the needs of modern society.
He was active internationally in the important roles with which he was entrusted by Pope Paul VI, as president of the Council for the Promotion of the Laity and the Commission on Justice and Peace.

His modesty, discretion and hard work made him a figure who reflected the grandeur of this country.
All Canadian men and women are proud of him.
We pray God that he may rest in peace.

From October 8 to 23, Mr. Speaker, I had the honour to accompany the Canadian delegation to the opening of the UNESCO's 23rd General Conference which is being held in Sofia, Bulgaria, until November 12.
In view of the serious crisis which the organization is facing, Canada's speech was eagerly sought after by the member countries generally.
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the House that the Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Vezina) made quite a remarkable speech on October 21. As a matter of fact, comments heard immediately following her speech confirmed that hers was undoubtedly one of the very best speeches because it outlined perfectly the ills that are undermining UNESCO's credibility and raised plainly the basic issues which the Conference should address.
Contrary to what was reported the next day by the France Presse news agency, whoever makes an honest effort and carefully reads the Minister's speech, just as Angele Dagenais did in the October 26 issue of the news paper Le Devoir, realizes that although Canada is dissatisfied with the situation which exists today within UNESCO, it will continue to adhere to this organization.
In view of the fact that the United States has withdrawn from UNESCO, and because the United Kingdom has openly indicated its decision to do likewise immediately after the Conference, this organization really needs Canada which will be called upon to play an increasingly greater role.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAX ON UNLEADED GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since spring the price gap between unleaded and leaded gasoline has gone from 2.5 cents to three cents per litre. The taxation on gasoline which is recommended by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget will widen the gap between leaded and unleaded gasoline prices even further because a lower tax is imposed on leaded gasoline than on unleaded. In making unleaded gasoline more and more expensive relative to leaded gasoline, the Minister of Finance is in effect rewarding the polluters.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) seems silent, unaware, or indifferent. He should impress on the Minister of Finance the fact that leaded gasoline affects health and that it is the policy of the Government of Canada to reduce acid rain emissions by shifting consumption in favour of unleaded gasoline. Therefore, the thrust of the Budget measure affecting gasoline should be reversed so as to impose a smaller tax on unleaded gasoline and a greater tax on leaded gasoline, achieve parity in the price of both gasolines, and wipe out misfueling.
The Minister of Finance is wrong in imposing a tax on unleaded gasoline which is greater than that on leaded gasoline because it will encourage greater use of leaded gasoline, thus increasing air pollution and acid rain damage at a time when the Government proclaims its intent to reduce acid rain damage. The Government is not practicing what it preaches.

October 29, 1985
Oral Questions PASSPORTS

subtopic: RECOMMENDED LISTING OF PHARMACISTS AS GUARANTORS FOR APPLICANTS
RECOMMENDED LISTING OF PHARMACISTS AS GUARANTORS FOR APPLICANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the years a number of pharmacists have been elected to this House. Many of them have quietly attempted to add pharmacists to the list of eligible guarantors for passport applications. Although there has been no change to date, pharmacists have continued to solicit the support of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark).
While no one disputes the qualifications of the existing list of eligible guarantors, many of them are not as accessible as a community pharmacist. How many people get to know personally their bank manager, lawyer, or veterinarian? Have you, Mr. Speaker, ever tried to get hold of your bank manager on a Friday night? How often do you see your veterinarian? Do you even know who is your local commissioner for oaths?
A recent United States survey indicated that pharmacists rank number two on a list of the most trusted community people. Pharmacists, by the nature of their profession, develop personal relationships with their customers. As professionals then, it would seem reasonable and logical for pharmacists to be added to the list of eligible guarantors for passport purposes.
I urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to consider recognition of pharmacists as trusted community leaders who should be added to the list of guarantors.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Would he be good enough to tell the House why it was he overruled the Minister of State for Finance and ordered a bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank in March? And will he tell us why he has stated consistently during the last seven months that he acted on the best advice available when it is clear he either did not have any advice at all or ignored the advice of the Director of Inspection of Banks, or he suppressed such advice? Why did he give this statement to the House of Commons?

Mr. Speaker, I gave the statement to the House of Commons because it was accurate. As my right hon. friend knows, the Government acted upon advice which was received. The Government considered that advice, decided it was appropriate and in the
national interest, governed itself accordingly, and will accept the consequences.
One of the reasons we appointed the Estey Commission, for example, was to provide an impartial review and permit fair-minded evaluations to be made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister admit that when he ordered the bail-out of the bank he did not have the facts because a proper audit of the books of the Canadian Commercial Bank had not been done, as it appears from evidence which was submitted before Mr. Justice Estey, or that the advice given to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance by the Inspector General's office was to the effect that, even on the basis of the information it had, the bail-out package was inadequate at that time? I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that we are all much smarter with hindsight; in fact, we are just about infallible with the benefit of hindsight. All I can tell my right hon. friend is that the Government acted on the best advice available from its public servants and from the officers of the Crown, which was considered by the Government of Canada and acted upon in the manner I have described.

raised by my Right Hon. colleague, but also on earlier facts which gave rise to the problems we know.

Mr. Speaker, we are back on the same track as we were on yesterday. The Hon. Member must realize that there is a purpose for the Estey Commission, and that is to consider the range of points of view that will be presented to the commission over the course of the inquiry. At that time, or possibly during the course of this inquiry, if members of the Government are called, we will have an opportunity to discuss some of the points of view. However, I caution the Hon. Member that it would be wrong, in relation to Mr. Justice Estey, for us to comment on individual pieces of information as they are presented to the commission.
Supplementary question.

Mr. Speaker, the only supplementary question to ask in light of that non-answer is to ask the Minister of Finance to confirm a rumour that he overheard the Prime Minister rehearsing In the Sweet By and By.
Order. The Hon. Member for Oshawa.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance which arises from the Auditor General's report which came out today. It has informed Canadians that there has been another billion dollar tax bonanza. According to the report, the former Government, headed by the present Leader of the Opposition, made a decision the day after the election was called to enable Dome Petroleum to get a billion dollar tax gift or concession.
The Minister of Finance spent all last fall admonishing Canadians about the problems of the national debt and suggesting that we had to cut back on social programs. Therefore, why did his Government announce in February an agreement confirming this billion dollar gift to Dome Petroleum?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, let us go back over the sequence of events. I believe it was in 1982 that the previous Government entered into extensive negotiations with Dome Petroleum and the chartered banks to provide support for Dome Petroleum, for a number of reasons about which I am sure the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice would enlighten the Hon. Member. It was pursuant to that, and pursuant to the announcement that Mr. Lalonde made in July, 1984, to the effect that a remission order would be granted on the basis of certain actions taken by the company. The company followed through on those actions and, because it did so, and in order to fulfil the commitment made by the previous Government, we acted on the basis that is set out in the Auditor General's report.
Mr. Speaker, to use an old phrase, the Minister of Finance had a choice.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance was not legally locked in. He could have renegotiated and used a number of options rather than giving away $1 billion of the taxpayers' money at a time when he was increasing taxes for ordinary Canadians across the land. Therefore, why did he give this $1 billion to Dome Petroleum?

Mr. Speaker, I ask the Hon. Member to think back to the circumstances. It was not a gift as the Hon. Member sets out, because if Dome Petroleum had been called upon to pay those taxes it would have gone bankrupt. If it had gone bankrupt it would have taken with it a number of the smaller oil services companies in the western economy that were suppliers of and had trade accounts with Dome Petroleum. That is a consideration that I ask the Hon. Member to take into account when he draws conclusions on this particular matter.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance knows that there are a lot of other options such as deferred taxes, special loans, and special Financial agreements through which Dome Petroleum would be obligated to pay back to the people of Canada the $1 billion it got, instead of getting the gift which the Conservatives gave it.

Since the Government made this unnecessary and wasteful decision about the taxpayers' money, will the Minister of Finance confirm that the Government did not even publish the details of that in February, but simply made a brief reference to the deal in what it gazetted, without telling the people of Canada that it cost taxpayers $1 billion?

Mr. Speaker, let me remind the Hon. Member that we were honouring a deal that had been entered into-

October 29, 1985
Oral Questions
You had an option.

The Hon. Member does not like the answer. He should listen to the answer and maybe he will learn something from it. We were honouring a deal entered into by the previous Government. We made the decision public at the time it was made. If the Hon. Member looks back he will see it in black and white.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. During his absence the former Deputy Minister of Finance revealed that the Gulf deal had been discussed a couple of times by the Priorities and Planning Committee which the Prime Minister chairs. Would the Prime Minister confirm that the Gulf tax ruling was in fact discussed by the Priorities and Planning Committee, contrary to the impression which he left at his press conference on October 11 ?

Mr. Speaker, I have the transcript of the October 11 press conference. It is entirely in keeping with what transpired. O&Y exercised the rights of any citizen under the Act to seek a ruling. The ruling was made by departmental officers, public servants, pursuant to objective criteria that exist under a statute which I understand was passed by this House under the Liberal Government. That is what transpired. Any discussion of any proposal was appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and has to do with the $1 billion gift his Government gave to Dome Petroleum on February 5, 1985. During the election campaign the Prime Minister, in no uncertain terms, told the former Prime Minister that he had a choice and that he should have disregarded the decisions made by his predecessor on patronage issues. Why then did the Government honour the commitment towards Dome Petroleum, which cost taxpayers $1 billion, instead of taking the option to renegotiate the deal?

Mr. Speaker, I have answered that question to the Hon. Member's Leader. We respected a deal that was made by the previous Government. The company had fulfilled its obligations under that deal. The Government of Canada was going to fulfil its obligations.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Finance if the Prime Minister chooses not to answer. When it came to patronage, his Leader said to the Leader of the Government at the time that he had an option and that the former Prime Minister should have rejected the patronage option. Why did you not reject this option and save the taxpayers a billion dollars in this bonanza to Dome?

Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister asking us to believe that a thousand million dollars of taxpayers' money can be drained from the public treasury without any consideration being given by him, the Minister of Finance or any other Ministers? If that is the case, how on earth is any control exercised over the finances of the country by the Government?

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals introduced and passed this legislation in the House of Commons. A taxpayer of the country, corporate or otherwise, came before the Department of National Revenue in the ordinary course of business and availed himself of the rights of any Canadian taxpayer to seek a ruling. That ruling was granted objectively pursuant to those criteria which govern in such cases and are determined upon by public servants, and public servants alone, acting in the public interest. That they were able to make such a finding was because of a piece of legislation which existed empowering them to so do. That piece of legislation was enacted because of the desire of the Liberal Government.

Mr. Speaker, because there was not going to be a savings of a billion dollars as the Hon. Member sets out. The fact is that if Dome Petroleum had not received the remission order, as had been promised by the previous Government, that company was not going to exist. It would not exist to pay the taxes that are foregone as a result of this remission order.
There are lots of other options.
As a result, the oil service industry in western Canada-
Lots of choices.
-which was under a great deal of pressure at the time-
Like the banks.

-would not have survived either, because there were a tremendous number of companies in that industry that had trade credits out to Dome Petroleum and they would have gone under as well.

October 29, 1985

It would seem that the Department of Veterans Affairs is one of the most recent victims of the May budget move to blindly and savagely cut jobs in the federal Civil Service. Recent reports show that 218 jobs will be abolished by next May. Could the Minister comment on the accuracy of such reports, and if such is the case could he tell the House how he will go about achieving the increases and improvements in services to veterans which he has so often been referring to this last year while slashing some 6 per cent off the overall staff? This is absolute inconsistency, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. George Hees (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to the Hon. Member's question I would advise him-and I think he knows this-that for the next six months there will be no lay-offs. Two hundred and nineteen positions have been declared surplus. Of that 219, 104 are either vacant or held by people who have already indicated their intention to retire, or are held by people who were hired on a term basis. We can see that only 114 positions are affected. I assure the Hon. Member that the Department will do everything possible in the next six months to find alternative employment for those people.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister has always been seen as a Conservative gentleman with very liberal behaviour and manners.
Could he tell us exactly what he intends to do, in order to specifically help the victims of those cuts by a Government that is in the process of committing hara-kiri? Is he bent on concluding his prestigious political career by making himself known as the hatchet Minister?
Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80 implements the budget proposal concerning the federal sales tax and excise tax and the excise duty as announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his May 23rd budget.
The Bill moves in four major directions.
First, pursuant to the recommendations made by the Nielsen Task Force, this Bill would enlarge the sales tax base, putting an end to a trend that leaves only 30 per cent of possible profit subject to federal taxation.
Second, this Bill would implement one component of the Government strategy to reduce the deficit by increasing the federal sales tax rate.
Third, this Bill would implement the election promise to eliminate automatic indexation of the taxes on alcohol and tobacco, an indexation which would have increased the taxes by 4 per cent in September and by an indexed amount over the coming years. In lieu of indexation, there will be a tax rate increase of 2 percent on alcoholic beverages and a 25-cent tax on the 25-cigarette package.
Finally, this Bill introduces an extensive system for assessing the objections and appeals under the Excise Tax Act. This new system is similar to the current one under the Income Tax Act, and includes recent improvements made to that Act with respect to search and seizure and the presumption of innocence
that prevents seizure until the taxpayer has a chance to resolve any litigation as to his Fiscal responsibility.

Before I continue with my remarks with respect to Bill C-80 I want to say that, in the true spirit of practical reform of some of our parliamentary procedures, the budgetary reform process is also of paramount importance. Some five months and six days after being introduced on May 23, 1985, we are still debating our first full federal Budget. I Find this a bit strange since we are effectively running the largest business in the country without having all of our fiscal plans in legal place. Some of my constituents, in fact, are asking me why we have not voted on all of the Budget yet and I find that sometimes difficult to answer. What I feel we should be looking at-and I know the Government is and will be looking at it more closely-is limiting and perhaps regularizing the Budget debate in future.
I would like to continue on a bright note and to end on an even brighter one. The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) said in the House last Thursday, October 24, and I quote from page 7941 of Hansard:
Early this week the Royal Bank of Canada confirmed that economic growth in this country is proceeding at a steady pace, that inflation and interest rates will continue to decline and unemployment will be at its lowest level in years. The Royal Bank says that the Canadian economy is looking better because Canadian businesses are spending more money producing more goods and employing more people.
The Minister went on to say, and I quote from page 7943 of Hansard:
I said it was a tough Bill but I believe it is also fair. It asks all Canadians to share in the effort to restore the fiscal health of our country.
I could not agree more. The Economic Council of Canada said in one of its recent reports that the real growth is expected to continue for the next four to five years in a very positive way in Canada. The Conference Board of Canada recently revised its growth projections upward for 1985-86 by a full 2 per cent of GNP increase. This is bright news and it is getting brighter every week. The Throne Speech spoke of national reconciliation and economic renewal and we are on track with both of these two national themes. The economic statement of November 8 spoke of a course of action to create jobs, growth and opportunities. If we look at the recent record of this Government, we find it has been simply remarkable. The Budget of May 23, 1985, builds on our successes to date by creating more opportunities through encouraging private initiatives and incentives in a realistic, fair and effective way. The fiscal course we have set is obviously working so far and will continue to work well into the future. All Hon. Members of the House know deep down that all of the economic news is good news.
Bill C-80, which represents one slice of the over-all budgetary process, concentrates on revenue raising measures from federal tax changes on candy, confectioneries, soft drinks, pet food, beauty and health goods, gazoline, beer and wine, construction materials, tobacco and a few other products, but the
October 29, 1985

over-all theme we must maintain is budgetary control of the deficit and its reduction through fiscal responsibility.
In the fall of 1984 I did a survey in my riding and I asked my constituents to tell me what they thought the top priority should be for the new Government. Three out of four of those who responded-75 per cent-indicated that deficit reduction was at the top of their list. I remind the House that we are exercising deficit control through and 80 per cent reduction of Government expenditures and only 20 per cent through tax increases. That is pretty responsible management, in my opinion.
Let me compare Bill C-80, in an over-all broad context, to an expandable swimming pool full of money-sometimes called "capital". Those who want to dive into this pool of money, the people who would use these funds, are you and I, Mr. Speaker, my constituents, businesses inside and outside of Canada-that is, the international community-and municipal, provincial and, obviously, federal levels of Government. We are the largest player in the pool and as our capital needs become greater, we squeeze out others from competition. That is bad because Governments do not create jobs, they create the environment for others to create jobs. Today's environment is now healthier than it has ever been. We compete for a part of that capital pool. The greater the competition to buy or borrow, the higher the price, and the price of money is interest. Therefore interest rates would probably rise unless we could lower our needs for our part of the pool. We cannot expand the size of the pool very quickly because it would mean printing more money or more capital. That could be inflationary. The over-all amount of money in the pool can only expand as the over-all wealth of our nation expands. With the elimination of the hideous National Energy Program, replaced by the very successful Western Accord, the very negative Foreign Investment Review Agency, replaced with a well received Investment Canada; and with capital gains incentives in the Budget, our over-all wealth is increasing and will continue to increase, thereby giving the Government more room to manoeuvre.
Since we cannot expand the size of the pool too quickly, we must lower our demands and swim in a smaller part of the pool so that others who are competing for those funds, such as businesses and other borrowers, will have a little more room.
Bill C-80 necessitates some of the changes we must make in order to allow the Government to have more financial flexibility. On the surface, the waters may look a little rough, a little tough, in fact, as it was said this morning, but fair. No one likes tax increases, myself included, but underneath the waters are much calmer. Our plan is obviously working. One can see the increased confidence levels in the private sector as it finds more areas to swim in and therefore the price of borrowing money is lowered.
1 can see the western energy developments are increasing tremendously in western Canada. The automobile industry of Ontario is operating near capacity. The housing industry is undergoing a tremendous uplift in new housing starts. The manufacturing industry is showing tremendous growth as consumers buy more and more durable goods.
Excise Tax Act
As the Miniser of State for Finance said with respect to Bill C-80, it is a tough Bill but it is fair in that all Canadians are asked to contribute. We must keep in mind the over-all budgetary themes such as economic growth. Recent economic indicators are all strong; deficit reduction, 80 per cent through expenditure reduction and 20 per cent through tax increases; and job creation, especially our great achievement in lowering the unemployment levels of the youth of our country in the last few weeks and months.
An area of real concern with which 1 have to deal in my riding concerning Bill C-80 is the increased taxation of construction goods manufactured other than at a construction site, such as steel, concrete, asphalt and even asphalt shingles for roofs, and others. A number of businesses in my riding reacted against the date of the proposed increase of July 1, 1985. They wanted to put it off until January 1, 1986. I met with a lot of these business representatives, with officials from the Department and discussed the issue with the two Ministers concerned who listened very attentively, but it was decided that the federal Treasury needed the revenue as soon as possible.
Normally these increases are effective immediately a Budget is brought down. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, the measures in the Budget were put off for a period of about six weeks in order to allow for a reasonable adjustment by the affected businesses. 1 find that very fair. The affected businesses in the construction industry were not questioning the need for the Governemnt to raise more revenue. They were merely asking for the effective date to be put off to January 1. They understood that we had to start to live more within our means. I think everyone in the House understands, as do my constituents, that we have to do the same. Mr. Speaker, what happens to you when you live beyond your means and for how long can you do that? You get a phone call from the bank. You are told that your credit is up, that you must turn in the plastic and have no more credit cards. On September 4, 1984, the people of Canada called up the former Government and said its credit was up, it was time for a change. They wanted to give the Tories a chance to run the business. Our track record to date is simply outstanding, but the struggle continues. The passage of Bill C-80 will give us more financial freedom to do more for those in the greatest need in Canada.

1 can only say that I regret that, but I am grateful that I spent some time in comments with the Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) which allowed me to dispose of some items.
Even though the Government is a little over a year old and Parliament convened less than a year ago, one can already have moment of deja vu.
Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, imposes increases as a result of the Budget of last May 23. There is an increase of 1 per cent in the rate of federal sales tax on various products, effective January 1,
1986.	There are other changes as well. For example, there is the extension of the federal sales tax on a variety of products enjoyed by men, women, boys and girls across the country. They will face increased charges for such things as candy, confectionery, soft drinks, pet foods and certain health goods.
There is tax on energy conservation equipment from a Government that claimed to be concerned about this matter. It is imposing sales tax on energy conservation equipment soon after it ended programs that supported energy conservation in this country. On that point alone, surely we have evidence of how reactionary this Bill is. There is also an increase of 2 cents per litre on gasoline and aviation gasoline, diesel fuel and aviation fuel which came into effect on September 3. There will be an additional increase of 1 cent per litre on January 1,
1987.	These tax increases go well into the future.
As I contemplate these increases I am reminded of the debate we had in the first weeks of this Session of Parliament. The Government had to consider the question of whether to go through with an increase in the sales tax which the previous Liberal Government had planned for October 1. It was surely very significant of what the Government would continue to do, that instead of cancelling that particular increase as it had
given every indication it would do before its success in the election-it was very critical of that Liberal sales tax increase-it decided to proceed with that 1 per cent increase. The following May, in the Budget measures we are debating here, the Government decided to add to those increases in sales tax. We have in the last minutes been considering the fairness of all this. It is not simply a question of fairness, but a question of the economic wisdom of following this course in the fiscal and financial policy of the Government.
There is a deficit, which is very significant. Why do we have a deficit? This Government will answer first by saying that too much is being spent. The Government does not very often say that there is a deficit because not enough taxes are being raised in certain areas, although in the practice of the Budget and in the Bill, C-80 that we are debating today, there is a suggestion that the people of Canada, as far as sales and excise taxes are concerned, should pay more. There is a deficit then, at least in part, because the ordinary people who already bear and excessive burden of taxation need more burden laid on their shoulders.
What has not been considered at all is the distinct possibility that there is such a large deficit in our federal fiscal operations because the Government of Canada has increasingly slipped into allowing various kinds of activity, particularly on the side of capital investment, to escape taxation. This has resulted in the rich getting richer, succeeding more and more in concentrating their economic power while the poor keep paying more and more taxes. That comes from a Conservative Government which likes to think it speaks for ordinary Canadians, that it is anxious about them and wants to ensure that prosperity genuinely comes to Canada.
It is not simply a question of fairness as I have said. It is also a question of economic sense. When you decide that the largest part of the burden of taxation is going to be borne by individuals who have to pay the sales and excise taxes willy-nilly, whatever they may want to do, they face these charges when necessities need to be purchased. They are sneaky taxes because they are hidden charges. As a rule they are simply in the price and there is no way of knowing what they were originally unless you check the charts.
There is little opportunity to appreciate exactly how serious these charges are as they get worked into the cost of things and percentages are added to them in additional charges. It is a matter of economic stupidity to make individual Canadians the basis for the fiscal system in this way. These are exactly the people on whom we depend to ensure business is being done in our communities, that people come into the shops with money to spend and buy things. That purchasing power gets translated into demand to wholesalers, factories and employment throughout our industries. If we insist on using these means to add inexorably year by year to the burden individuals have to bear, then we will find, as we have found in the past decade and a half, that all the inducements we may provide in the way of our tax expenditure system, accelerated capital cost allow-
October 29, 1985

ances and so on, do not succeed in ensuring that there is enough investment taking place to give us anything like full employment. What it does, Mr. Speaker, is to make the rich far richer than they would be otherwise and to reduce more and more of the Canadian population to poverty. That was obvious by the beginning of this decade when the Department of Finance provided some evidence of the benefits that federal tax expenditures amount to for Canadians at various income levels. On the basis of the 1979 returns, Canadians who had incomes of $7,500 to $10,000, obviously very poor Canadians as far as the demands of life in our cities and towns are concerned, were receiving over $300. It was well under 5 per cent benefit as a percentage of income. But Canadians who had incomes of over $200,000 were receiving benefits that exceeded $50,000.
An individual Canadian in the existing system, which dates back to the early 1970s and which has been quite fundamental in creating the deficit situation we have, could receive in tax expenditure benefits more than the total income of five or six other Canadians. There is the rank unfairness of the system which the Liberals created through the 1970s and early 1980s and which to date the Conservatives have done absolutely nothing to change.
There is the ultimate foolishness, the economic stupidity, with what we are faced in Bill C-80. We want the Bill taken back. We want the Government to come to grips with the fact that tax expenditures may well be running at the $30 billion to $50 billion level, meaning that the deficit impact of these tax expenditures may be as much as $15 billion, almost 50 per cent more than the total deficit the Government is presently running. If that were the case, we would have the clearest of arguments for an actual reduction in taxation for invididuals. We would have an argument for reducing the sales tax, not increasing it. What would happen at the same time the Government came to grips with tax reform as it should and if the Government recognized as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated last November? Let me quote his statement:
As we grapple with the technicalities, the subtleties and the complexities of our tax system, we must never lose sight of the citizens it is ultimately meant to serve. That is what our efforts are all about. The real bottom line is people.
I could not agree more with that Mr. Speaker, but where is the action that is required to operate on this statement?

Mr. Speaker, I am also proud and pleased to take part in this discussion.
In my view, Bill C-80 probably is since the Progressive Conservatives came to power the document that best depicts and defines the true faces of those men and women who are now at the helm.
This Bill enables us to understand how and where the Government team wants to lead this country over the coming years. Let me say first that we all admit and accept the fact that the national debt is tremendously large, that it requires
Excise Tax Act
and deserves particular intention, so that steps will be taken to eventually reduce that deficit.
On the other hand, we all admit that this country has had to go through an historically unprecedented period in every respect, and Canada did so in a way that is simply fantastic, and at the end of that crisis, steps had to be taken to restore and straighten out our public affairs. And today we are witnessing the impact, the spin-offs of measures that were put forward by the previous administration. We see the levels of job creation and inflation-
On the other hand, Hon. Members opposite suggest: "Listen, if interest rates went down, if inflation abated, if there is job creation, it is because of measures, of initiatives we have taken since we came to power on September 4." But this is my view is not the case, and it is certainly not where that improvement is concerned.
To me, the important thing today is to get into details, and see the true orientation which this Progressive Conservatives Government wants to impart to the country.
We now have before us Bill C-80, the basic aim of which is to collect taxes, to extort money from the smallest people possible, middle and small income earners, the have-nots, those who find it most hard to make ends meet under current condition.
In this context, they put forth Bill C-80 in order to pick money from small people's pockets, the purpose, of course, being to collect $15 billion or so.
In other words, middle and low-income taxpayers are being asked to bear the whole burden of our financial problems in
Canada.
It would be both unacceptable and just as unbearable, but it would nevertheless keep up the pretence of some sort of justice if, at the same time and in the same breath, the Government told the wealthy, those with substantial means, that they must also make an effort and do their share to reduce the deficit.
However, that is not the point. The point is that, with Bill C-80, the Government is going to take millions of dollars away from the poor, from those with very low incomes, and give this money to multinationals, to individuals who can pay and who have made it through the recent crisis without any problem.
In this regard, I believe that it is important and relevant to list some of the initiatives which favour the wealthy in Canada. If I may, I would just like to mention the capital gains exemption with which the Government tells those who make profits in real estate or on the stock market: The next few years are going to be highly profitable years for all you Ladies and Gentlemen who are involved in big business. During the next few years, you will be allowed to claim as non-taxable income up to $500,000 in capital gains for Personal Income Tax purposes. It is assumed that you will re-invest that money

Excise Tax Act
in the system. But what guarantee do we have that you are indeed going to do so? All Hon. Members are aware of course that the taxpayers who are going to benefit most from these generous provisions are not those who are living in poverty and who can hardly make ends meet. The taxpayers who will benefit most are those who are well-off, if not outright rich, and who could, without depriving themselves of the necessities of life, make a special effort to reduce the national debt. I feel this measure is quite unfair for all middle-income Canadians.
There is another matter which I find especially odious. We are dealing today with Bill C-80. Well, the same Minister, namely, the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) introduced recently Bill C-79 to ask Canadians for SI billion to compensate these honourable gentlemen and corporations who had invested in a bank at very favourable rates in excess of the $60,000 of normally fully insured deposits. The Government needed $1,000 million to reimburse these people all the money they had invested in these Western banks, capital and interests, and for that purpose the Government introduced Bill C-79, the legislation that was immediately followed by Bill C-80 we are now studying.
In the following Bill, Bill C-80, the Government is telling people who can hardly make ends meet: Ladies and gentlemen, you will have to play your part to help the Government meet its obligations. You will have to tighten your belt. You will have to do your share by paying a surtax or a higher tax so we can meet our obligations. This is happening right after another Bill to raise $1 billion to repay individuals and companies that, in many cases, will take the money and invest it outside Canada, in foreign countries where it will not do anything at all to spur the Canadian economy.
Well, Mr. Speaker, barely 14 months have elapsed and this Government is giving us today an opportunity to see how it is reacting to the vote of confidence and support it received from Canadian men and women last September 4. Although we have been talking about the Bill for several days, I remind the people of Canada and the House just exactly what we are talking about. The federal sales tax will be increased by 1 per cent as of January 1, 1986 if the Bill passes. Canadians would be interested in knowing what rate they will now be faced with as far as the new rates are concerned. For example, they will be paying 7 per cent on all construction materials, 7 per cent on cable and pay television services, 14 per cent on alcoholic beverages, 14 per cent on tobacco products, and 11 per cent on all other taxable items. It is very interesting to note that the whole process will cost Canadian consumers $990 million in 1986-87.
Today the Auditor General brought down his annual report. One item in it concerned something done by the Government on February 5, 1985 when it gave a remission to the Dome Petroleum company. This will cost Canadian taxpayers in the next 10 years something over $1 billion. Dome Petroleum will not have to pay taxes for the next 10 years which is going to cost us something over a billion dollars. That is considerably more than the total revenue from all these taxes. There was an alternative to this taxation. The Government had an option, to use the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It did not have to pass that remission. It could have taken equity in Dome Petroleum so that at the end of 10 years we would have an equity of a billion dollars in that company, or it could have given it a loan. It had an option but it chose instead to give Dome Petroleum, the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, a billion dollars. This money is derived from increases in excise and sales taxes on the ordinary Canadian.
The federal sales tax is being expanded as well. Sales tax exemptions on candy, confectionery, soft drinks, pet foods and certain health foods and energy conservation equipment are repealed. All of those items, which have been non-taxable up until now, are going to be taxed. These are areas where the ordinary Canadian spends a little bit of money for his comfort or his recreation.
The excise taxes, which are direct taxes added on to the prices and not a percentage tax, not an ad valorem tax as the

With this one cent on January 1, the two cents on September 3 and the past increases in fuel over the last year, instead of a 20 cent reduction per gallon that the farmers were promised they have instead a 20 cent increase per gallon in the cost of fuel. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to oppose this Bill for a number of reasons. First, when we are talking about sales taxes, we are talking about taxes that are regressive and place a more severe burden on lower-income earners than on people with higher incomes. People with lower incomes spend a greater proportion of their incomes on the basic necessities of life including food, clothing, shelter and other things needed to carry out a daily existence. Therefore, when it comes to sales taxes, people with lower incomes are hit more severely by increases. This was confirmed by a recent study carried out and released by the National Anti-Poverty Organization. Regarding this study, an article in The Globe and Mail reads as follows:
The study says that those estimates "make it clear that the poorest of Canadians will pay increases in federal sales and excise taxes at twice the rate paid by the most affluent families."
The article is quoting a study done by the National AntiPoverty Organization. It is not a political group. It is not a supporter of any political party. It speaks objectively about the plight of lower income Canadians, the poorest Canadians, all across the country. Yet, when the Government decided to obtain more tax revenue, not for expanding programs to help lower income Canadians but to reduce the deficit, it decided to place an undue and unfair share of the burden in reducing that deficit not on the backs of well-to-do Canadians but on the backs of the poorest of Canadians through measures such as Bill C-80. As we know, the Budget increased and expanded federal sales taxes, according to the press report with respect to the study of the National Anti-Poverty Organization, "by raising the rate on such items as construction materials, alcohol, tobacco and extending coverage to such other items as candy, pet food, many health and personal care products and insulation materials". Is that not the height of insensitivity and lack of concern for the needs of lower income Canadians? Even the candy bought by children on the way home from school is to be hit by this additional sales tax.

speechtext: Shame.

I thank Hon. Members of the House for their consideration. Mr. Speaker, Canada is a rich land and Canadians are productive people. Yet, one-sixth of the people of Canada, according to a recent report, are living in poverty as it is understood in our country. One of the chief causes of this poverty is the lack of decent, affordable housing. The Government of Canada can lead the way to remedying that lack and, therefore, I shall propose a plan to ensure that every Canadian can have decent, affordable housing. After I have outlined my plan I shall explain my reason for it which arises from the failure of the privately run real estate and housing industry to meet this goal. Finally, I shall show why I believe my plan is financially workable.
The first principle of the plan is that housing for Canadians shall be decent and affordable. By "decent" I mean in accordance with the standards of CMHC for health and safety standards. That means it would include weather-tight shelter, no crowding, proper bathroom and kitchen facilities and modern heating and lighting. By "affordable" I mean it would
cost the residents no more than one-quarter of their income for rent and utilities.
The second principle is that both publicly owned and privately owned rental housing shall be subject to rent control. Since a growing number of Canadians live in cities-about three-quarters of Canadians in fact live in cities-and the majority of those in multiple dwellings owned by absentee landlords, mainly the large corporations, tenants need a statutory basis for organizing in order to bargain on more equal terms with their landlords to attain reasonable accommodation and service for reasonable rent. Therefore, the federal Government, in the course of negotiating cost-sharing programs with the provincial and other jurisdictions, must ensure that the best use of federal moneys is made by negotiating for rent control and rent registry. Rent levels must be registered with Governments and the information available to tenants and prospective tenants. There must be no exceptions, either because of public ownership or because of rent level.
The third principle is that Canada must create a national home-building program. The federal Government must negotiate with the other jurisdictions, according to needs in each, to devise a program aimed at creating, in five years, the half a million units needed by the families and singles presently without decent, affordable housing. In order to control costs and ensure responsible maintenance this housing should be either co-operatively produced and owned or public produced and owned with as much management responsibility as possible assumed by the tenant associations.
The fourth principle is that existing substandard housing should, where practical, be rehabilitated with Government assistance. Tens of thousands of rental apartments in Canada's major cities need rehabilitation because federal tax benefits have encouraged builders to throw buildings together fast but not to do maintenance. Roofs and garages are leaking and plumbing, heating and elevator systems are breaking down. To allow the absentee owners 20 per cent or 25 per cent permanent rent hikes, as is proposed, in order to increase the owner's equity by rehabilitation, would, therefore, be compelling the tenants to pay once through rents and once again through taxes which would be a massive injustice. It would also depress the tenants' buying power for food, clothing and other necessities that Canadians earn a living by producing. Therefore, Governments must devise ways to assist tenants to buy their buildings for co-operative or non-profit ownership and that way to ensure a motivation for responsible maintenance and taking the buildings out of the inflationary market, somewhat in the manner of utilities like schools, roads, and public hospitals.
The fifth principle is that private homeowners must also receive aid to remedy the damage done to them by the same land, interest and tax squeeze that has made tenants poorer. Public loan funds must be established, or private loan funds within Government legislation, that will provide mortgages to homeowners at no more than 2 per cent above the rate of inflation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I had been speaking for approximately eight minutes and 1 was saying that the sixth principle of the program I am proposing is that there should be annual targets and reports. The federal Government shall, after negotiations, publish jointly with the other jurisdictions the outline of the five year plan with annual targets. Parliament and other jurisdictions and the public will be encouraged to debate this plan for possible amendment and adoption. Thereafter they shall jointly publish an annual report showing progress toward the targets, the numbers of men and women employed in construction, maintenance and management, relations with labour unions, and the growth of co-operatives and non-profit corporations.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the substandard housing produced in such large numbers by the present housing and real estate industry is itself, of course, not the main cause of poverty. The main cause is low income. However, substandard housing also contributes heavily to poverty.
I would like to give some examples of how bad housing deepens poverty, increases poverty and makes poverty harder to overcome. In the Northwest Territories, for example, according to a survey made a year ago as many as 11 people in some settlements were living in two bedroom bungalows with leaking roofs and faulty wiring, often sleeping in shifts to compensate for the fact that there were too few beds. There is an increase in family violence, assaults between spouses, in breakdowns of families and in high school drop-outs. There is a zero vacancy rate for rental units in Yellowknife. Waiting lists there contain up to 100 names for a single apartment when there is a vacancy. In other words, life is being damaged by bad housing.
In Toronto, a recent Metro Social Planning Council report said that the high cost of rental housing is leading to hunger, sickness and emotional trauma for many of Metro's most vulnerable and disadvantaged households. This is in Toronto where the vacancy rate in the city is .03, or three apartments or houses out of 1,000 for rent. The result is malnourishment of the children and neglect in families. There are more than 20,000 men, women and children waiting for subsidized housing in Metro. There are more than 4,900 families and 441 seniors on the waiting list for the Metro Toronto housing authority units. Children have been placed, of necessity, into foster homes only because their parents' homes were too crowded to help them. Yet this year, City Non-profit Housing and Metro Toronto Housing Company Limited could only build 300 new units each. We are not nearly keeping up with the need.
In Halifax, it is stated that the vacancy rate for rental housing in the Metro area has consistently been below 1 per cent since 1981. The average cost of a three-bedroom apartment is between $550 and $750, yet the poverty line of $20,000 would mean such a family should probably have only

October 29, 1985
Housing
about $410 to pay for rent. Four hundred and ten dollars could not possibly get a three-bedroom apartment, which a family of four very likely needs, depending on the age of the children. They have asked for assistance to build 1,000 social housing units this year because only 252 were constructed in the last five years. Again, the result has increased homelessness- families of four and five persons are living in one room- increased family breakdowns, and increased child abuse. Physical and mental health is being affected. There are unnecessary hospital admissions and food money is spent on shelter. There is frustration of human service workers, and this does not come only from the poverty itself and the lack of income of those people, it comes from the housing and the condition of that housing. The point is we have to arrive at the understanding that housing, like education and health service, is a necessity for Canadians to provide so that Canadian children can grow up as a healthy part of this country.
One more point in regard to the effect of housing itself on poverty, Mr. Speaker. Over one-sixth of Canadians were below the poverty line in 1984, that is, half of the single elderly and half of the singles under 25 years of age, but the gap between rich and poor also widened during the last four years. What this means is that every year there are more people who are in poverty, and those are nearly always the same people who are damaged by the substandard housing.
Let me now outline how the real estate and housing industry, helped by the federal Government, so misdirected and squandered the wealth and revenues of Canada over the last generation that many hundreds of thousands of house and apartments fall below the national standards of health and welfare.
First, the land. Land prices for housing have risen crazily since World War II in most cities, where three-quarters of Canada's people live. Prices often jump by 10 times over 10 years, five times faster than wages. The land sharks defend this price gouging as the natural, inexorable product of the impersonal market. But we know from experience that that argument is unparallelled, unmitigated, and self-serving balderdash. It is politicians in Government who help their friends in business by spending huge sums of taxpayers' money on roads, railroads, port and airport installations in a way so as to enable land owned by their friends to fetch a higher price. Tenants and homeowners must pay twice, once in their taxes and again in rent or mortgages because the Government will do nothing to set a ceiling on prices.
Look at Toronto's Dome Stadium, Mr. Speaker. The CNR, a Crown corporation, is giving $50 million worth of public land to private corporations so that they can skim a profit. They plan to build luxury office buildings around it, maybe luxury condominiums and a few luxury rental apartments, although the rental vacancies in Toronto are .03 per cent. Offices, which Toronto needs like the bubonic plague, are several hundred times higher in their vacancy rate. People are not renting offices but that is what the builders build. Many condominiums are going unsold. Why is the land not donated for low rental housing instead?
Second, interest rates. Since the federal Government 18 years ago lifted the ceiling off housing mortgages, the banks have increased the 2 per cent spread between what they pay for the money they invest and what they get for it. They have increased it to as much as 6 per cent, 8 per cent or 9 per cent, triple or more the take. No wonder no more than one Canadian in five can now really afford to start buying a house.
The federal Government, which enjoys restraining workers and small business, ought to begin by restraining the banks. Even if the Government cannot control inflation rates, it can and must stop the banks from pushing inflation higher through extortionist interest charges on mortgages.
