Mr. Speaker, by way of introduction, I should like to ask the Hon. Member where he stood when the "Clark" Government of 1979 introduced the mortgage interest deductibility feature and was partially defeated on it. I assure him that such a program was not designed for the rich. It was designed to make housing available to those people who were having difficulty finding suitable housing.
However, the Government welcomes the motion of the Hon. Member, for it raises some very important matters upon which we have acted during the past year. Of course I am referring
October 29, 1985

to the housing review and consultation process. This process involved and continues to involve the active participation of the provinces, representatives of municipal interests, natives and many other important players in the housing sector. Moreover, one of the key purposes of the process is to develop better ways of ensuring that Canadian in need have access to affordable, adequate and suitable shelter. Today, and in recent weeks and months in the House, the Hon. Member has raised some important questions about the consultations and about the directions of federal housing policies. On behalf of the Government, and in particular the Minister responsible for CMHC, I will take this opportunity to address some of those questions and to speak generally about the housing consultations and policy directions which are emerging.
A good place to begin is with the question as to why the housing consultation process was undertaken. The answer in large part was indicated in the economic statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in November of last year. At that time the Government committed itself to renewing the strength of our economy. To do this, we pledged to put our own fiscal house in order and to get control of the deficit. We also set out to improve co-operation between the two main levels of Government and to get Canadians in general working again in pursuit of national goals. These objectives bear directly on housing.
When the new Government assumed office a year ago, federal housing expenditures were on the rise. There was a pressing need to get those expenditures under better control and to ensure that limited funds were expended efficiently and effectively. There was also a clear need to improve federal-provincial co-operation in housing. Housing is one of those areas in which both levels of Government have roles and some very important responsibilities. At times we had programs working at cross purposes, as well as duplication in programs and administrative overhead. This created confusion in the minds of the people the programs were supposed to help. It also increased the costs to both Governments and of course to Canadian taxpayers.
The housing actions of Governments also created problems for the housing industry. There was particular concern about the "on again-off again" programs initiated at both levels of Government. What the industry needed was reasonable stability and certainty in its operating environment. It wanted the federal and provincial Governments to commit themselves to a common approach, a common game plan. It wanted the federal and provincial Governments to consult, to co-operate and to co-ordinate their housing activities. All it was asking for was a stable housing environment within which to operate. It was certainly not an unreasonable request.
There is one further point about federal-provincial relations in housing which needs mentioning here. Over the last decade the federal Government has assumed on a national basis an increasingly larger share of social housing expenditures. In some provinces the federal Government has been bearing nearly all the costs of new activities.
Housing
Provinces must recognize their responsibility to act in partnership with the federal Government. This means that they must contribute their fair share to the costs of housing programs. The reasons I have just discussed for undertaking the housing review and consultations suggest the objectives toward which federal housing policies should strive.
In many speeches to housing groups in the last eight months to ten months, the Minister has outlined four objectives of the Government. One is to build a national consensus on appropriate objectives of federal housing policies and programs. Second is to design effective programs to meet those objectives. The third is to improve the relationship between the federal and provincial Governments in housing and remove needless duplication in the administration of programs. The fourth is to achieve a fairer balance on a national basis between federal and provincial housing expenditures. Considerable progress has been made toward achieving these objectives, thanks largely to the co-operative participation of the many housing interest groups as well as the provinces in the review and consultation process.
I will now outline some of the conclusions and directions which are emerging from this process. A consensus has been building around a number of objectives for federal housing policy. What Canadians have been telling us is that the paramount purpose of social housing programs should be to assist households that cannot afford decent shelter; that federal housing policy should aim to strengthen security for home owners and prospective home owners through steps to foster private market development of longer term, fixed interest rate mortgages; that the Government should ensure continued access to mortgage funds in all parts of the country; and that moderate-income households unable to afford home ownership should have opportunities for security of tenure.
The next question concerns programs to meet those objectives. In the case of social housing, it is generally accepted that there is a need for a mix of programs involving the construction or acquisition of housing, the provision of assistance to enable households to pay market rents, and the rehabilitation of substandard low-cost housing to bring it up to minimum standards. If the most cost effective solution is to be put in place, flexibility to apply these approaches in different proportions across the country is required.
In the consultations it was generally felt that the federal Government could take steps to help Canadians achieve the security they desire through home ownership. This assistance can be achieved by the federal Government working with the private sector to create an environment for the development of long-term, fixed rate mortgages. There is universal support among housing interest groups and the provinces for mortgage-backed securities, which will contribute to the develop of longer term, Fixed rate mortgages. The Government has indicated that it intends to proceed with a mortgage-backed securities program.
There was also strong support for the need to ensure access to mortgage funds on an equal basis across the country. Not

October 29, 1985
Housing
surprisingly, there was considerable suppot for the continuation of public mortgage insurance.
Another objective around which a consensus has been building is what the Minister has called opportunities for security of tenure for moderate-income households unable to afford home ownership. The Government recognizes that the co-operative housing movement has made a significant contribution to housing in Canada, and that many moderate-income households look to co-operative housing as a way of achieving their housing aspirations. The Co-operative Housing Foundation has put forward an innovative proposal for financing co-operative housing, and the Government is continuing to consult very closely with it on the proposal which involves the use of index-linked mortgages.
I have talked briefly on the merging consensus on appropriate objectives of federal housing policy and on programs to meet those objectives. I want to move on now and talk about the federal-provincial discussions in housing. Last December federal and provincial housing Ministers met in Ottawa and agreed to work together in a new spirit of co-operation and to examine housing programs to ensure that they are effectively targeted to those in greatest need, and efficiently delivered. I might note here that, under the previous Government, the last multilateral meeting of federal-provincial housing Ministers was held in June, 1981, some four years ago; whereas this Government has participated in two such multilaterals in the space of eight months.
The second meeting of federal-provincial housing Ministers was held in Calgary in early July of this year. The Ministers reached an agreement on a number of matters including acceptance of a report on market housing, a declaration of unanimous support for mortgage-backed securities and agreement to a set of principles to govern future federal-provincial territorial activity in social housing. These developments have led some to worry that the federal Government might be removing itself from social housing and simply turning it over to the provinces. I can assure those that might think that is happening that the federal Government has no intention of reducing its commitment to social housing.
The discussions that have been ongoing between federal-provincial housing Ministers and officials have focused on ways of co-ordinating federal and provincial initiatives, of overcoming duplication between Governments and rebalancing, on a national basis, the relative expenditures of both levels of Government.
The set of principles on social housing agreed to at the July conference did include the principle the provinces may deliver social housing under conditions acceptable to both levels of Government. From the federal point of view, those conditions include assurances that federal housing objectives are met and that mechanisms are in place to ensure federal accountability.
There should be no doubt about federal objectives nor about the Government's commitment to ensuring that its objectioves are met. Regardless of what happens in program delivery,
there will remain the need for the federal and provincial Governments to continue to work together and plan social housing strategy.
In addition to concerns about future federal-provincial roles in social housing, there have been charges from some who should know better that the review and consulation process has not been open and fair, that groups interested in housing have been excluded from the process. There is absolutely no truth to this. From the start, the Government was committed to an open process and welcomed, indeed encouraged, the participation of all interested parties. I think a look at the process that has been followed clearly demonstrates this fact.
In late January the Minister released a consultation paper on housing. It was intended to stimulate and focus discussions during the consultations. About 8,000 copies of that paper have been distributed to date. The response to it has been substantial. In fact, it has been overwhelming. The Minister has received over 300 briefs and letters from a wide range of interested parties including social policy and service organizations, local tenant associations and co-operative housing groups, native associations, business groups, representatives of municipal interests and many individual interested Canadians. Also included among the respondents were all of the major housing interest groups.
Following receipt of the briefs the Minister and myself began a series of personal meetings, most of which took place in March and April of this year. The purpose of these meetings was to clarify issues in the briefs and to discuss housing generally with the groups. These meetings have involved the participation of some 21 different groups. The participants included industry association, social housing groups, financial organizations and groups representing women, the poor, the elderly, the disabled and natives.
In all cases, though, regardless of whether meetings with interested parties took place, responses to briefs and to the many letters were provided. Over the summer the responses were closely analysed and it was then that the Minister turned to intensive consideration of the housing direction that the Government might pursue.
Furthermore, subsequent follow-up meetings have been held by the Minister's staff and senior CMHC officials with major interest groups. The purpose of these meetings has been to inform the groups about federal-provincial discussions, to respond further to proposals contained in their briefs, and to outline and discuss possible directions that we might take.
I want to tell the Hon. Member, because I know he has a special interest in native housing, that native groups are among those with whom the Government is closely consulting. The Minister has received a number of briefs and letters from native organizations across the country. He has met twice now with the Native Council of Canada and has extended an open invitation to the Assembly of First Nations. In addition, members of the Minister's staff and senior CMHC officials have met with the Metis groups and the Inuit groups of Canada, as well as with the NCC and the AFN. The views and
October 29, 1985

concerns of native groups are being taken into full account in the housing review.
The openness and co-operation that has been displayed in the consultations will not be lost. The Government intends to continue to rely on the co-operation of all those involved in the housing sector as we proceed to develop and put in place policies and programs that effectively and efficiently meet the housing needs of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, the housing policies and programs that this Government will develop and implement will be widely accepted because they will have evolved out of the input of all interested Canadians. Those policies and programs will be the products of consultations promoted by a Government that listens and then acts.

Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the motion I would like to comment on the remarks of the Progressive Conservative Member who just spoke about consultation. Perhaps they are trying to make people believe that the Government is concerned about social housing and housing generally, but we have to remember that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) tabled a document last November, and that the first step taken by this Government was in the sector of social housing where they slashed $9.6 million off the envelope for social housing, cooperatives, low rental units and nonprofit organizations.

Here is what the Progressive Conservative Government did with respect to two programs which had been very popular for a number of years because they were designed to improve housing in Canada: cutbacks of $29 million in RRAP, Mr. Speaker, and the people of Quebec had to bear the unfairness of those measures taken by the Government. Unfortunately all Quebec Conservative Members did not say a word about this.
Mr. Speaker, cutbacks amounted to $17 million in Quebec, as compared with only $2 million in Ontario.
As we recall, Mr. Speaker, this decision was made before the elections in Ontario and we know it was a political manoeuvre to try and save Mr. Miller's neck, but the people saw through this scheme and threw out Mr. Miller and the Ontario Conservative Party.
Mr. Speaker, in this field the previous Government always saw to it that funds were available to improve the quality of

housing and create jobs. The funds available under RRAP were quite useful and even necessary in Quebec and the Maritimes, while Ontario and the western provinces were spending funds allocated under rental unit construction programs. That was the request. Mr. Speaker, the consultation now going on is only a sham. The people in Quebec have not even been able to meet the Minister. They had to be content with the fellow who carries his suitcase, the Parliamentary Secretary. In addition, this meeting could not even be held in French in Quebec. Yet, we all know that Quebec has always been to the forefront as far as housing, cooperative, rehabilitation and repair programs are concerned, that it has innovated in this field under governments of all parties, whether under the Liberals of Robert Bourassa, when I was Member of the National Assembly with my colleague, or under other administrations. Quebecers have always been innovators.
Yet, there is no Quebecer in the consultation group, no Quebecer to take part in the decision-making process. Quebec was ripped off by the Prime Minister when the RRAP and the social housing program were axed.
Mr. Speaker, if we really want to have an effective and healthy policy for housing, we have to stop using band-aid solutions. First, it is essential to hold a national conference and include all those involved in this field. For the moment, the Conservative Party is content to meet its friends who own multiple unit buildings. Of course, and I do not blame them,
they want to make some money, but they forget that they have tenants. We should do what was done in the case of pension reform by Miss Begin and Mr. Allen MacEachen, the former Minister of Finance, who organized a national conference to discuss the issue of pension reform with all the interested parties. As long as there are secret consultations, apparently by the Minister responsible for housing, but in fact by a task force led by the Deputy Prime Minister, the Government should say so and stop lying to people. The national conference on housing should include architects. They have a lot of impact on the cost of residential construction. The conference should also include young families who could suggest mechanisms to provide ownership opportunities to young couples who want to look forward to the future. Why is it that, as the Hon. Member seems to be trying to say, and I know what he means as I was Parliamentary Secretary for housing, and the Hon. Member has read the text prepared by the officials, will it be suggested that there be a 50 per cent cutback in social and cooperative housing and that this money be used instead for housing subsidies?
Mr. Speaker, if there is no rent control in a given province, a housing subsidy would simply mean that the landlord would increase the rent and the taxpayers' money would go directly into his own pockets. On the other hand, if the housing subsidy is given only to tenants, what will happen in all the rural areas where there are small homeowners who cannot make both ends meet?
Cooperatives therefore were essential and needed to house senior citizens who had low income, had worked all their lives and received small pensions, for they were not accepted in social housing units and did not have enough money to live in residences where rents are higher and geared to more affluent people. So they got together in housing cooperatives or nonprofit corporations which made it possible for all people with average income to find accommodation in homes for the elderly where they felt secure because these were new buildings offering protection and various facilities.
The federal-provincial link should also be discussed at those meetings, at this national conference. I happen to know that the Government of Quebec wants the Canadian Government to hand over all such funds so that the province might allocate them as it sees fit. I met with most Quebec groups responsible for cooperative housing and nonprofit organizations, and they all say no. I can tell you that some of them voted yes in the referendum, but in this case they say no, we need protection and the low rental housing sector in Quebec must be administered by the province.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say it is imperative to debate the housing issue, and I dare hope that the Government will put an end to its pseudo-inquiry and set up a true national housing conference.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-WELLAND CANAL BLOCKAGE-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF SHIPPING SEASON
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-WELLAND CANAL BLOCKAGE-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF SHIPPING SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I wish to address this evening is one I raised with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) in Question Period on October 21 having to do with the upgrading of the Welland Canal section of the St. Lawrence Seaway. The blow-out of Lock 7 on October 14 has served to focus attention on the need to look again at upgrading the canal facilities. We now know that the canal will be open on November 6. The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority is to be commended for the fast action taken in repairing the damage. Notwithstanding this, the matter of upgrading the canal is one which must be addressed.
The recent accident has affected all of the communities along the canal. Sailors have been laid off and industries, both local and across the country, have been affected. Detractors would have us believe that the canal has outgrown its usefulness. That is not true. According to statistics gathered by the Canadian Trade Commission, 26 per cent of Canadian goods are transported by truck; 32 per cent by rail; but fully 40 per cent of Canadian commodities are shipped by water. There is no indication that this will change. Water transportation is cheap, fast and efficient and it will continue to be that way if we maintain our waterways to international standards.
I would like to take a few moments to outline briefly some of the history of the canal. 1 think it is important for Hon. Members to realize what this engineering marvel has done for the country's development. When the first Welland Canal was completed in 1829 it provided the means to bring grain cheaply and quickly from the interior of the country to the St. Lawrence River and on to Europe. One forgets what an incredible achievement it was and is to have conquered the obstacle presented by Niagara Falls, making it possible to link the Canadian West along 2,200 miles of continuous inland waterways to the Atlantic Ocean.
Since 1829 the canal has been rebuilt four times. The first canal included 40 locks. Later this was reduced to 27 locks and still later to 26 locks.
At the turn of the century, a report of a Government-appointed commission which said that wheat, lumber, copper and iron from the upper lakes would pass through the canal in
Adjournment Debate
increasing amounts were it not for the fact that larger boats of the period could not go through the then existing canal resulted in the 20-year construction of the present waterway which was opened in 1932 and which became generally known as the fourth Welland Canal.
For this fourth canal a new route was chosen which would take ships across the Niagara Peninsula in virtually a direct north-south line of only 26 miles. The difference of 326.5 feet between the levels of Lake Ontario and Lake Erie was overcome by seven lift locks and one control lock. Three of the seven lift locks are twinned, thus allowing ship traffic to move in both directions simultaneously.
Improvements have been ongoing over the years. In anticipation of the opening of the St. Lawrence Seaway in 1959 the depth was increased to 27 feet. A sophisticated control centre was installed in 1966 and it is being updated this year. The most important improvement, however, was the $200 million Welland Canal bypass which was completed in 1973. The old nine-mile stretch of the Welland Canal which bisected the city of Welland and imposed a navigational problem for the new and larger ships was abandoned and replaced with a new bypass.
This project took seven years to complete, during which period I was mayor of the city of Welland. 1 am, therefore, very aware of the immense amount of work which went into this realignment project not only to the canal itself but to the railway and road systems which were taken under the new channel by means of tunnels.
The completion of the bypass channel allows lakers 730 feet long to travel through the Seaway locks. What a difference this is from the 100 by 20 foot vessels which used the first Welland Canal.
1 hope through this brief historical outline I have illustrated how ongoing improvements to the Welland Canal have kept it up to world engineering standards. The Seaway's corporate plan, however, indicates that the Welland Canal will not be able to handle the increased demand which will be placed on it in the future in terms of both the number of ships using the canal and the larger size of ships which will be in use in the 21st century.
The corporate plan indicates that the capacity pressures will surface in about 15 years, around the year 2000. That is not a long time away, Mr. Speaker, for improvements to be planned. The recent accident at Lock 7 is currently holding up 107 ships in the Great Lakes system. The financial losses this is causing to the Seaway, shipping companies and suppliers are running at a very high level. I therefore suggest that the Seaway authority consider a program of upgrading the lock system at an early date.
A necessary part of this process would be a cost benefit analysis of proposals which have already been made. These proposals include three conceptual plans for lock improvements. One plan is a new system of superlocks in a new location which would lower the number of locks to three, as

October 29, 1985
Adjournment Debate
well as widening them for larger vessels. The necessary land was purchased in the three communities at that end of the Seaway in 1975 but the project has since been placed on hold.
The second plan is the conventional twinning plan which would twin locks numbered 7, 3, 2 and 1 in the same manner as the flight locks 4, 5 and 6. Here again, the necessary land is in place.
The third proposal is the hybrid twinning plan which also calls for the existing locks to be twinned but with longer and wider locks to accomodate the larger ships of the future.
As these plans are already drawn up, and considering the importance of the canal to Canada's future economy, I would like to ask my question again, this time to the Parliamentary Secretary. In light of the recent accident and in light of the future demands which will be placed on the current facilities, will these proposals be given serious consideration with a view to implementing one of them in the near future as the Government looks at improving the Welland Canal?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY-WELLAND CANAL BLOCKAGE-REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF SHIPPING SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the importance attached to this waterway system, of course the Minister will give very serious consideration to the proposals put forward by the Hon. Member this evening and which have been reiterated by him on a number of occasions.
I would like to take the opportunity to briefly indicate to the House, first, that because of the uniqueness of the accident of the blow-out-the fact there was no history to rely on- congratulations are probably in order to the officials of the Seaway, the contractors, subcontractors and the men who actually worked on the site for the splendid and 1 feel very responsible and professional way they effected the repairs. Concrete will be poured into the blow-out hole commencing later today, if it has not already been done. We are indeed optimistic that the reopening date of November 6 not only will be met but will be exceeded. Hopefully we might have ships moving prior to that date. There are 107 ships in the system. We can move these at the rate of about 24 or 25 a day so it will take about a week to clear up the backlog and return the activities of the Canal to normal.
To address very briefly the contingency plans that have been put in place, the House will be aware that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) have made the offer and, indeed, grain will move assisted by CN which will locate and operate grain hopper cars east of Thunder Bay. The Government, in its wisdom, and to facilitate the movement of this product, will assist in the payment of any additional costs that are incurred. We are very pleased with the progress of the repairs. Those involved with them are to be congratulated.
With respect to the cause of the blow-out, I do not think we will know that with any certainty for some time to come. The detailed analysis will take quite a while. I thank the Hon.
Member for his suggestions and reassure him that the Minister and the Government will take them seriously.

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVES-GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO TASK FORCE REPORT. (B) REQUEST THAT CO-ORDINATING AGENCY BE ESTABLISHED
CO-OPERATIVES-GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO TASK FORCE REPORT. (B) REQUEST THAT CO-ORDINATING AGENCY BE ESTABLISHED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity of saying something more this afternoon about the importance of co-operative development in Canada. Two weeks ago today I asked the Minister responsible for liaison with co-operatives (Mr. Mayer) about a Government response to the report of the National Task Force on Co-operative Development. I was not satisfied with his answer at the time, but I feel honoured today to have him in the House to respond further in the minutes that he has to this report. 1 really do look forward to him saying good things about what the Government plans to do.
In the minutes that lie before me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say something about the importance of co-operatives and to underscore the importance of a substantial federal response. Mr. Ray Siemens, the President of the Co-operative Union of Canada, wrote to all Members of Parliament early this year sending along copies of A Co-operative Development Strategy for Canada which dates from May of 1984. He sent a memorandum with that, the second paragraph of which reads:
The new government has indicated that its primary objective "is to put in to place a policy framework that will release the creative energies of Canadians to build a better future for themselves" and challenged Canadians to participate in wide-range consultations about this framework and the future direction of our country.
He goes on to indicate that people involved with co-operatives in Canada were very happy to have that invitation and joined in the consultation. I am aware that those discussions continue.
The report itself, A Co-operative Development Strategy for Canada, makes a number of points that I think help us to appreciate how very important co-operatives could be to achieving just what the Government set out in the fall of 1984 as its own objectives. On page 5 of the report it reads:
Pairing the democratic responsiveness and economic efficiency that characterize co-operative business, we believe that co-ops can play a key role in Canada's national development. As serious as the new problems are that face Canada, they also open many opportunities for new development. We have identified four such areas where co-ops can make a difference. Worker-owned co-operative businesses offer a direct means of meeting the often desperate need of many Canadians for jobs and a sense of control in their lives. The rapidly increasing costs of health care systems are straining government finances; co-operative health care delivery systems provide an attractive and affordable solution. Fisheries co-ops are an overlooked, yet critical part of the solution to problems facing the fishing industry. And in meeting the demand for affordable housing in this country, the co-operative model has proven to be a successful alternative and could be expanded to the benefit of many Canadians.
The report focuses on these four areas. In scanning the 32 recommendations which this task force arrived at last year for developing co-operatives in Canada, I will note those that deal specifically with matters that the federal Government could support.
October 29, 1985

Therefore, in connection with worker co-operatives, I note that Recommendation No. 12 focuses the importance of a support system which could provide the encouragement that workers need to develop co-operative policies for control of their industry. In fact, I might point to Canadian Porcelain in Hamilton as an example of such a development being undertaken or approached last spring. I do not believe it would be unfair to the Government to express regret that the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion did not ensure that that project moved ahead.
A support system established under this recommendation and, as Recommendation No. 13 says explicitly, the endorsement of the federal Government having been given to such possibility, we would see worker co-operatives as one of the means by which individual Canadian workers in their communities and work-places could have a larger role in the direction of their work-place and could actually see a return in the gains in which they participate.
Recommendations Nos. 15 and 16 deal with the matter of health care, specifically the possibility of health co-operatives. In both cases, they call for federal Government participation. It is suggested that it would be very useful to have a substantial conference to explore this, since these possibilities have in fact been demonstrated by community clinics. It would be useful to have such a conference, with the Federal Government playing its part in funding it. It would also be useful, as Recommendation No. 16 suggests, to establish a development assistance group in this area. Again, the federal Government could play a very useful part.
There is the question of housing and the importance of co-operative housing in this country. Recommendation No. 23 suggests that that be continued. I understand that the federal Government appreciates the importance of this sector. I realize that another Minister is responsible for housing and I am very pleased to hear that progress is being made.
The fourth area that this task force singled out concerns the matter of fisheries co-operatives. There are a number of recommendations that help us to appreciate more of the challenge that faces the Minister, who is here this afternoon, and the federal Government. It is important that co-operatives receive similar financial treatment as the conventional capitalistic enterprises with which we are familiar. Surely worker co-operatives should not be discriminated against simply because they are co-operatives.
There is the matter of the establishment of a central division in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the importance of technical resource groups.
Although I may have started a minute or two late, Mr. Speaker, may I conclude by suggesting that with respect to Government support generally, it is important that the federal Government take up the recommendations, specifically Recommendations Nos. 30, 31 and 32. I look forward to hearing the Minister talk about the progress he is making in finding personnel and establishing exactly how the federal Government plans to move ahead in providing a response to
Adjournment Debate
this matter. He has already indicated that he fully appreciates its importance.

subtopic: SOCIAL AFFAIRS-INCREASED ROLE OF VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL DISCUSSIONS
SOCIAL AFFAIRS-INCREASED ROLE OF VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I directed several questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I pointed out that an increasing number of people were finding it necessary to depend on voluntary agencies for food baskets, for meals and for clothing. I asked the Minister whether it was not time to discuss with his counterparts in the provinces what was wrong with the social security system established over the years since the end of World War II; why so many people seem to be falling through the cracks in the system and why so many people are having to depend on charity. I urged the Minister to work with the provincial Ministers to improve and expand the Government programs so that people would not have to depend on charity.
In the last 40 years, since the end of World War II, we have developed a whole host of programs which we thought would meet the needs of Canadians; for example, the unemployment insurance program, the pension programs, the medical and hospital insurance plans and the provincial social welfare programs, funded in part by the federal Government. Most Canadians believed that we established a system which would meet the needs of Canadians.
As unemployment has grown in recent years, and we have seen the number of unemployed people increase to 1.5 million or over 10 per cent, we have witnessed a growth in the voluntary effort. Last week it was brought to the attention of the people of Canada and to Members of Parliament by the National Council of Welfare that over four million Canadians now live in poverty, or 17.8 per cent of the population, and that the number of low-income children under the age of 16 years has risen steadily each year from 1980 onward, so that we now have 1.2 million children living in poverty, or one child in five is poor. I could continue with those Figures. The situation is unacceptable to me and should be to all Canadians.
We have seen in every city, town and village in every province from the Atlantic to the Pacific tremendous growth in the number of voluntary church, native and community groups which have established food banks so that people can obtain the food baskets, the meals or the second-hand clothing which they need. We know that in many cities some children get their first meal of the day at noon at the school they attend, and that some can only attend school after being given used clothing obtained at one of these voluntary centres. I believe Canadians in need should not have to depend upon charity. I give a great deal of credit to them and respect the efforts of voluntary organizations, but I believe the needs of Canadians should be met by government programs, provided as a right.
I call upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to work with provincial Ministers to upgrade and expand our existing assistance programs which are partially funded by the federal Government through the Canada Assistance Plan, so that those in want will again have their needs met by government programs, to which I believe they are entitled, and that the generous efforts of the voluntary groups can be cut back as they become less necessary.
I call the attention of the Government to the recent study conducted by the National Anti-Poverty Organization in which it was pointed out that the increase in the sales and excise taxes included in the May Budget had very adverse effects upon the poorest of Canadians. It pointed out that these taxes would cost each Canadian family several hundred dollars a year, and that the poor, or those with incomes of less than $10,000 per year, would pay twice as high a percentage of their income as wealthy Canadians with incomes of $50,00 or more. NAPO has proposed that the Minister of Finance establish a refundable federal sales and excise tax credit for those in low-income brackets. I urge the Minister of Finance to give careful and sympathetic consideration to that proposal of the National Anti-Poverty Organization.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SOCIAL AFFAIRS-INCREASED ROLE OF VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS. (B) REQUEST FOR FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL DISCUSSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the concerns of the Hon. Member-concerns which certainly are and ought to be those of all the Members of this House-regarding the number of Canadians living in poverty, and also to point out to the Hon. Member what is being done by this Government to combat poverty, without, of course, overlooking the increasingly important role played by charitable organizations.
We want to combat poverty in two ways. First of all, we want to take the direct approach by providing increased employment opportunities. Second, we are taking steps to improve financial support for those who are most in need.
We realize that Canadians want to work. During our first year in Government, 304,000 jobs were created. We have set up a number of projects aimed at improving opportunities for employment. For instance, the Canadian Jobs Strategy announced by Miss MacDonald was set up after consultations
October 29, 1985

with Canadians. Certain elements of this strategy are specifically aimed at improving the employment potential of certain Canadians whose chances of entering the labour market would otherwise be very slim.
In addition, the federal Government has recently reached an agreement with the provinces and the Territories to increase labour market opportunities for social assistance recipients. This agreement will make support under the Canada Assistance Plan and the Canadian Jobs Strategy more flexible while helping welfare recipients to develop skills and experience to assist themselves.
During our first year in office we have also been combatting poverty through initiatives to provide more financial assistance to those who are most in need. For example, by extending the Spouse's Allowance Program the Government has increased the income security of an estimated 85,000 widows and widowers aged 60 to 64, the majority being widows.

As a more direct response to the concerns of poor families with children, the Government, Mr. Speaker, has consulted
Adjournment Debate
with Canadians and produced a series of changes in child benefits, in its May Budget. These changes will provide increased benefits for families who are least well-off, including low-income families, by raising the ceiling of the child tax credit to $524 per child over the next few years.
We are also taking other steps to upgrade income and job securities, and I am thinking of the employment equity legislation.
Mr. Speaker, generally speaking, the measures taken by the Government to provide for economic renewal and recovery, job creation and reform of social programs, clearly demonstrate our concern and our commitment to fighting poverty in Canada. By improving our economy and our general economic productivity, we will be able to provide all Canadians with a more secure future in which they will have a better chance of making a decent living.
